items.title: I told the model to separate fields with <TAB>. It did exactly that, and I lost 79 percent of my data.
items.summary:
My extraction prompt said: Output lines of the form The model output: Elizabeth I have not the pleasure of understanding you Those are five literal characters — angle bracket, T, A, B, angle bracket — not a tab. My parser looked for \t , found none, and dropped the line. Across one document, 246 of 310 records were discarded . Only 5 were dropped for the reason the mechanism actually existed to catch. The model did what I asked. I asked for the wrong thing. Why I did not notice for a whole benchmark run This is the part worth stealing, because the bug is trivial and the reason it survived is not. My harness counted discarded records in a single field called rejected . That field had one documented meaning: a record whose evidence could not be verified against the source text . In other words, it was the hallucination-catching counter. So the run printed rejected=246 and I read it as the verifier working hard . A parser failure was wearing the costume of a successful integrity check. The number went up, and up was the direction I wanted. The fix is not a better parser. It is that these two things must never share a counter: unparseable — our format failed, the model is not at fault ungrounded — the model asserted something that is not in the text One of those is my bug. The other is the model's. Summing them produces a number that cannot be acted on, and which flatters whichever explanation you already believe. After splitting them, the same run reads: records: lines=310 kept=64 | unparseable=246 ungrounded=5
separator: canonical=0 tab=64 literal_TAB=246 There is no way to misread that. Fix one: show the delimiter, never name it A model can reproduce a character it can see. It cannot reliably reproduce a character you have described in prose, because your description is text and copying text is what it does. So instead of naming the separator, I showed a worked example using a pipe. I picked | after checking the corpus contained zero of them in 7,987,517 characters. Result: canonical separator compliance went from 0 to 9 out of 9 on the first fragment, and unparseable loss went from 79 percent to zero. Fix two: your example must be obviously not data The first version of that fix failed differently, and worse. I used a real line from the source novel as the worked example: Elizabeth | I have not the pleasure of understanding you The model copied the example verbatim and extracted nothing else. One line of output for a 60,000-character fragment. It looked plausible. The name was a real character, the quote was real dialogue. The only reason I caught it was that the evidence verifier rejected it — that sentence is not in the fragment I sent, it is from a later chapter. The working version uses a name that cannot appear in any novel and says so: Zolvane | we must leave before the tide turns

That line is ONLY a format example. Zolvane is not in this text; never copy
the example into your answer. A worked example is an instruction to imitate. If your example is indistinguishable from valid output, some fraction of the time it will be returned as output. Fix three: make the failure loud, at the right granularity I added a check that aborts when more than 20 percent of output lines have no recognised separator, printing a sample of the offending line. My first version aborted the whole document. That was worse than the bug: the model follows the format on most fragments and abandons it on a few, so discarding the document threw away every good fragment along with the bad one. Four documents produced zero records. Now a violation fails one fragment . Good fragments survive, the failure is still visible and still blocks a headline answer, and one document went from zero records to 148 of 169 kept. The forty-second diagnostic The single highest-value thing I added was a --probe flag: run one fragment, print the raw model reply verbatim, print the loss breakdown, exit. It takes about seven seconds. It caught both the literal- bug and the example-copying bug immediately. Before that, my shortest path to noticing a contract problem was a full benchmark run — about forty minutes — and even then only if I read the right counter and interpreted it correctly, which the first time around I did not. If your pipeline sends prompts to a model in a loop, you want a way to see exactly one of them, unedited, in under a minute. I wrote three throwaway scripts to do that by hand before admitting it should be a flag.

items.title: GPA Scales Do Not Convert. Building a Calculator That Admits It.
items.summary:
GPA Scales Do Not Convert. Building a Calculator That Admits It. Every GPA calculator eventually gets the same feature request: "can you convert my 8.6/10 to a 4.0 GPA?" The obvious implementation is one line: const converted = ( gpa / fromMax ) * toMax ; // wrong, and confidently so This is linear rescaling, and it is wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with arithmetic: the scales are not measuring the same thing at the same resolution. What the scales actually are A grading scale is a mapping from letter or percentage bands to numbers. The bands are not evenly spaced, and they are not the same across systems: US 4.0        A = 4.0    B = 3.0    C = 2.0    D = 1.0    F = 0
              (a letter covers ~10 percentage points, roughly linear)

India 10.0    often  CGPA ≈ percentage / 9.5,  but institution-specific
              (the divisor is a convention, not a conversion)

France 20.0   14/20 is a strong result; 18/20 is exceptional and rare
              (the top of the scale is deliberately almost unreachable) Rescaling a French 14/20 linearly gives 2.8 on a 4.0 scale — a US "B−". Anyone familiar with both systems will tell you a 14/20 is a considerably better result than that. The error is not in the multiplication; it is in assuming both scales use their full range the same way. French grading compresses the top deliberately. US 4.0 grading does not. The same applies going the other way. A 10.0-scale CGPA of 8.6 mapped linearly is 3.44, but many Indian institutions publish a conversion of CGPA × 9.5 = percentage , which gives 81.7% — and 81.7% is not a 3.44 in most US conversion tables either. So what should a calculator do? The honest answer is: compute within a scale, and be loud about conversion between them. Within a scale , GPA is well-defined and worth computing precisely: it is Σ(grade_points × credits) / Σ(credits) , and the only real complexity is credit
weighting and how the institution rounds. Between scales , there is no universally correct function. There are institutional
conversion tables, and they disagree with each other. A calculator that silently applies linear rescaling is producing a number that looks authoritative and is not. One that supports multiple scales natively — 4.0, 4.3, 4.5, 5.0, 7.0, 10.0, 20-point, percentage — lets a student compute in the system they are actually graded in, which is the number they actually need. The weighting bug that is much more common Conversion is the flashy problem. The bug that bites more people is credit weighting. // wrong: unweighted mean, ignores credit hours const gpa = grades . reduce (( a , g ) => a + g , 0 ) / grades . length ; // right: credit-weighted mean const gpa = courses . reduce (( a , c ) => a + c . points * c . credits , 0 ) / courses . reduce (( a , c ) => a + c . credits , 0 ); The two agree only when every course carries identical credits — which is true in some high school systems and false in essentially every university. A student taking a 1-credit seminar and a 4-credit core course does not have those two grades count equally, and a calculator that says otherwise gives a number the registrar will never produce. Then there is weighted vs unweighted in the US high school sense, which is a completely different meaning of "weighted": AP/honours courses map an A to 5.0 instead of 4.0. Both concepts are real, both are called weighting, and conflating them in the UI produces support emails forever. They need different words in the interface. Rounding is a policy, not a detail 3.4950 displayed as 3.50 versus 3.49 decides scholarship eligibility at some institutions. There is no neutral choice here: Round half up, round half even, or truncate — all three are in real use Round once at the end, or round each semester and then average the rounded values —
these give different answers Some institutions cap the displayed GPA at the scale maximum, some let weighted values
exceed it A calculator cannot know which policy applies. What it can do is not hide the choice: show enough decimal places that the user can see they are near a boundary, rather than silently rounding them across it. What I would tell someone building one Compute the credit-weighted mean. Always. The unweighted version is a different
statistic and almost never the one asked for. Support scales natively instead of converting into one canonical scale internally.
Round-tripping through a canonical scale loses information at every hop. If you offer conversion at all, label it as an estimate and say which table you used. Use different words for "credit-weighted" and "AP/honours weighted" in the UI. They are
unrelated concepts that share a name. Show one more decimal place than you think you need. Boundary cases matter more than
precision looks like it should. None of this is difficult code. It is mostly the discipline of not producing a number that is more confident than the underlying data supports — which, for a tool students use to make decisions about their applications, seems like the minimum bar. If you want the credit-weighted version without writing it yourself, the calculator is here — it computes on the scale you are actually graded on rather than converting you into one.

A grading scale is a mapping from letter or percentage bands to numbers. The bands are

US 4.0        A = 4.0    B = 3.0    C = 2.0    D = 1.0    F = 0
              (a letter covers ~10 percentage points, roughly linear)

India 10.0    often  CGPA ≈ percentage / 9.5,  but institution-specific

with both systems will tell you a 14/20 is a considerably better result than that. The
error is not in the multiplication; it is in assuming both scales use their full range
the same way. French grading compresses the top deliberately. US 4.0 grading does not.

The same applies going the other way. A 10.0-scale CGPA of 8.6 mapped linearly is 3.44,
but many Indian institutions publish a conversion of CGPA × 9.5 = percentage, which
gives 81.7% — and 81.7% is not a 3.44 in most US conversion tables either.

So what should a calculator do?

The honest answer is: compute within a scale, and be loud about conversion between
them.

  • Within a scale, GPA is well-defined and worth computing precisely: it is Σ(grade_points × credits) / Σ(credits), and the only real complexity is credit weighting and how the institution rounds.
  • Between scales, there is no universally correct function. There are institutional conversion tables, and they disagree with each other.

A calculator that silently applies linear rescaling is producing a number that looks
authoritative and is not. One that supports multiple scales natively
— 4.0, 4.3, 4.5, 5.0, 7.0, 10.0, 20-point, percentage — lets a student compute in the
system they are actually graded in, which is the number they actually need.

The weighting bug that is much more common

Conversion is the flashy problem. The bug that bites more people is credit weighting.

// wrong: unweighted mean, ignores credit hours
const gpa = grades.reduce((a, g) => a + g, 0) / grades.length;

// right: credit-weighted mean
const gpa = courses.reduce((a, c) => a + c.points * c.credits, 0)
          / courses.reduce((a, c) => a + c.credits, 0);

The two agree only when every course carries identical credits — which is true in some
high school systems and false in essentially every university. A student taking a 1-credit
seminar and a 4-credit core course does not have those two grades count equally, and a
calculator that says otherwise gives a number the registrar will never produce.

Then there is weighted vs unweighted in the US high school sense, which is a completely
different meaning of "weighted": AP/honours courses map an A to 5.0 instead of 4.0. Both
concepts are real, both are called weighting, and conflating them in the UI produces
support emails forever. They need different words in the interface.

Rounding is a policy, not a detail

3.4950 displayed as 3.50 versus 3.49 decides scholarship eligibility at some
institutions. There is no neutral choice here:

  • Round half up, round half even, or truncate — all three are in real use
  • Round once at the end, or round each semester and then average the rounded values — these give different answers
  • Some institutions cap the displayed GPA at the scale maximum, some let weighted values exceed it

A calculator cannot know which policy applies. What it can do is not hide the choice: show
enough decimal places that the user can see they are near a boundary, rather than
silently rounding them across it.

What I would tell someone building one
  • Compute the credit-weighted mean. Always. The unweighted version is a different statistic and almost never the one asked for.
  • Support scales natively instead of converting into one canonical scale internally. Round-tripping through a canonical scale loses information at every hop.
  • If you offer conversion at all, label it as an estimate and say which table you used.
  • Use different words for "credit-weighted" and "AP/honours weighted" in the UI. They are unrelated concepts that share a name.
  • Show one more decimal place than you think you need. Boundary cases matter more than precision looks like it should.

None of this is difficult code. It is mostly the discipline of not producing a number
that is more confident than the underlying data supports — which, for a tool students use
to make decisions about their applications, seems like the minimum bar.

the calculator is here — it computes on the scale you are
actually graded on rather than converting you into one.

items.title: Comparing AI Evaluation Experiments: Measuring the Impact of Changes to AI Applications
items.summary: AI Engineering Fundamentals AI Evaluation · Part 7 ← Part 6 So far in this series, we have focused on one fundamental question: How good is our AI application? We started with deterministic checks, brought humans into the evaluation loop, used LLMs as judges, and eventually evaluated interactions happening in production. But evaluation becomes even more useful when we start changing the application. Maybe we changed the prompt. Maybe we switched models. Maybe we added a tool, changed retrieval, or moved part of the decision-making from the LLM into application code. Now the question is different: Did the change actually make the application better? Running a few prompts against the new version and checking whether the responses look good isn’t enough. A change might improve the behavior we were targeting while quietly breaking something that already worked. And with non-deterministic AI systems, even running the same example once can give us a misleading picture. The dataset stays the same. The evaluation criteria stay the same. The evaluator stays the same. The application change is the variable we want to measure. In this final part of the AI Evaluation series, we’ll do exactly that with Wayfinder our flight search application. We’ll establish a baseline, make a targeted engineering change, run the same evaluations again, and compare the experiments to understand not just whether the scores changed, but what behavior changed and whether the evidence is strong enough to support our engineering decision. Building a Focused Dataset for the Comparison But an overall score doesn’t always tell us what happened to the behavior we actually changed. Imagine we make a change to improve how an AI application handles requests with multiple constraints. The overall evaluation score improves. That sounds promising. But it leaves us with more important questions: Did the behavior we wanted to improve actually get better? And did that change break anything that was already working? To answer those questions, it helps to include examples that directly exercise the behavior we’re changing, along with examples that protect behavior that already works. This gives us two useful types of evaluation cases: Target case — exercises the behavior we expect our change to improve. Regression guard — exercises behavior that already works and that we don’t want our change to break. These focused cases don’t replace the application’s broader evaluation suite. They give us a clearer way to understand the impact of a particular change. Throughout this series, we’ve used Wayfinder our AI-powered flight search assistant, to build and explore different evaluation techniques. We’ll continue with the same application here as we move into experiment comparison. Consider this request: Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least available seats. Wayfinder has to do two things correctly here. First, it needs to consider only flights with at least two available seats. Then, from those flights, it needs to find the cheapest one. This is the behavior we want to study, so we’ll make it our target case . But there is another side to the comparison. Suppose our change fixes this request but somehow breaks a simpler request that Wayfinder already handles correctly: What is the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow? We haven’t really made the application better — we’ve just moved the problem somewhere else. So we’ll keep this simpler request as a regression guard . Our comparison dataset is therefore deliberately small: {"id": "cheapest_with_min_seats", "query": "Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least 2 available seats.", "expected_behavior": "Recommend the lowest-priced retrieved flight that satisfies the stated minimum seat requirement. Do not recommend a more expensive flight when a cheaper eligible flight exists."} {"id": "find_cheapest_flight", "query": "What is the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow?", "expected_behavior": "Recommend the lowest-priced retrieved flight for the requested route and date."} The first case asks: Did we improve the behavior we were trying to change? The second asks: Did we accidentally break behavior that already worked? Of course, two examples are not enough to evaluate an entire AI application. That’s not what we’re trying to do here. We already built broader evaluation coverage earlier in the series. For this experiment, these two cases give us a focused way to follow one change and understand its impact. And most importantly, we won’t change them between experiments . We’ll first run them against the current version of the application to establish a baseline . Later, after making our change, we’ll run the exact same examples again and compare the results. With the dataset fixed, we now need a way to run those evaluations as repeatable experiments. Running the Experiment Locally If you’ve been following the series and already have Wayfinder set up locally, you can skip the installation and environment setup below. Just make sure you’re on the version used for this experiment. The complete implementation used throughout this article is available in the companion GitHub repository . To follow along with exactly the same code shown in this article, check out the v0.6.0 release. This ensures the code, commands and screenshots remain consistent over time. To follow along locally, clone the repository and check out the release containing the online evaluation implementation: git clone https://github.com/DivakarUngatla/wayfinder.git cd wayfinder git checkout v0.6.0 Install the project dependencies: uv sync Before running the evaluation, configure the required environment variables. Create a .env file: cp .env.example .env Configure the required environment variables: OPENAI_API_KEY= LANGSMITH_API_KEY= LANGSMITH_TRACING=true Running Evaluations as Experiments We now have a fixed set of examples. The next step is to run them against the application and record the results in a way that lets us compare them later. We’ll do that by running the evaluation as an experiment . An experiment is a recorded evaluation run of a particular version of our application against a fixed dataset. For each example, the experiment: runs the application captures its response and the context it used evaluates that response records the results Later, after we change the application, we’ll repeat the same experiment with the same evaluation setup and compare the results. For Wayfinder , we’ve wrapped this workflow in a small experiment runner: def target(inputs): result = agent.run(inputs["query"]) return { "response": result.response, "retrieved_flights": [ flight.model_dump() for flight in result.flights ], } def evaluator(run, example): return judge.evaluate( query=example.inputs["query"], expected_behavior=example.outputs["expected_behavior"], response=run.outputs["response"], context=run.outputs["retrieved_flights"], ) The target is the application we're evaluating. LangSmith gives it an example from our dataset, and Wayfinder returns both the generated response and the flights it retrieved. The evaluator then takes that output and scores it against the expected behavior. We’re reusing the same LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator we built earlier in the series, so we’re not introducing a new evaluation technique here. We’re changing how we use the evaluation results: instead of looking at one run in isolation, we’re going to compare runs from different versions of the application. LangSmith’s evaluate() ties the pieces together: evaluate( target, data=dataset_name, evaluators=[langsmith_llm_judge_evaluator], experiment_prefix=args.prefix, num_repetitions=args.repetitions, ) The dataset gives us the examples. The target runs Wayfinder. The evaluator scores its behavior. And LangSmith records the results as an experiment that we can inspect and compare later. There is one parameter here that deserves some attention: num_repetitions=args.repetitions Why would we run the same evaluation example more than once? Because with an AI application, one successful run doesn’t necessarily mean the behavior is consistently correct. And that’s something our baseline experiment is about to show us. Establishing Our Baseline Before making any changes to the application, we need to understand how the current version behaves. This gives us our baseline — the reference point we’ll compare our change against later. We’ll run the two examples in our dataset five times each: python examples/experiment_comparison/compare_experiments.py \ --dataset-name wayfinder_experiment_comparison \ --prefix wayfinder-baseline \ --repetitions 5 The first time we run this command, the experiment runner creates the dataset in LangSmith from our local JSONL file. From then on, we’ll reuse this same dataset for every experiment in this article. With two examples and five repetitions, our baseline contains 10 evaluation runs . Why repeat each example five times instead of evaluating it once? Because a single successful response can give us a false sense of confidence. AI applications can produce different responses for the same input, and our LLM-based evaluator can vary as well. If a behavior works once, we know it can work. If it works repeatedly, we start learning something about how consistently it works. When the evaluation completes, the runner prints a link to the experiment in LangSmith. Let’s open it and look at what happened across the five repetitions. The simple cheapest-flight request works correctly in all five runs. The multi-constraint request is different: four repetitions score perfectly, but one fails. In repetition 3, Wayfinder recommends Japan Airlines JL703 at ₹48,550 with 12 available seats . But the retrieved flights also contain Air India AI302 at ₹41,000 with 6 available seats . Air India satisfies the same minimum-seat requirement and is cheaper. Wayfinder had the information it needed, but still selected the wrong flight. Your exact results may differ. Both the application and the LLM-based evaluator are non-deterministic, so you may see the incorrect recommendation in a different repetition — or all five runs may succeed. What matters is that we use the same evaluation setup when comparing the baseline with the version we change next. The interesting part isn’t that Wayfinder cannot handle the request — it gets it right in four of the five runs. The problem is that the same request doesn’t produce consistently correct behavior . Now we have something concrete to improve — and something concrete to compare our next experiment against. Finding the Right Thing to Change Our baseline showed us where the application sometimes fails. But before changing anything, we need to understand why . In the failed run, Wayfinder had already retrieved the cheaper Air India flight. So retrieval wasn’t the problem. The problem happens after retrieval. In the current implementation, the retrieved flights are passed to the response-generation LLM. The LLM has to apply the user’s constraints, compare the eligible flights, select the cheapest one and generate the final response. Conceptually, the flow looks like this: Retrieved Flights ↓ LLM ↓ Apply constraints Compare prices Generate response But filtering by available seats and comparing prices are deterministic operations. We don’t need an LLM to make those decisions. That gives us a simple engineering hypothesis: Move deterministic filtering and ranking into application code, and let the LLM focus on generating the response. The application would then look more like: Retrieved Flights ↓ Filter + Rank ↓ LLM ↓ Generate response We don’t know yet whether this change will actually improve the application. That’s exactly what our next experiment will measure. Moving Deterministic Decisions into Application Code Now we can implement our hypothesis. Wayfinder already uses an LLM to convert the user’s request into a structured FlightSearchRequest. We can extend that structure so the application also knows how the results should be ranked: passengers: int = Field(default=1) sort_by: Literal["price", "duration"] | None = None arrival_before: time | None = None For our target request: Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least 2 available seats. the extraction step now produces: { "source": "Bangalore", "destination": "Tokyo", "passengers": 2, "sort_by": "price", "arrival_before": null } The LLM is still doing something it’s good at: turning natural language into structured intent . But once we have that structure, the application can handle the deterministic decisions itself: flights = [ flight for flight in flights if flight.available_seats >= request.passengers ] if request.sort_by == "price": flights.sort(key=lambda flight: flight.price) elif request.sort_by == "duration": flights.sort(key=lambda flight: flight.duration) For our target request, this means Wayfinder first removes flights with fewer than two available seats and then sorts the remaining flights by price. The response-generation LLM no longer needs to perform that filtering or ranking itself. It receives flights that have already been processed according to the structured request and focuses on generating the response. So our architecture has shifted from: LLM → interpret constraints + make deterministic decisions + respond to: LLM → structured intent → deterministic application logic → LLM response The change looks promising, but we haven’t established that it actually improves the application’s behavior. To find out, we’ll run the same evaluation again and compare the two experiments We’ve only looked at the key parts of the change here. The complete implementation also handles additional filtering and ranking behavior and updates the response-generation flow accordingly. If you’re following along with the repository, switch back to the main branch to get the completed candidate implementation: git checkout main git pull This gives us the candidate version we’ll evaluate next. Our v0.6.0 checkout remains the reproducible baseline we started with. Running the Candidate Experiment Now we evaluate the changed application using exactly the same setup as our baseline . Same dataset. Same two examples. Same evaluator. Same five repetitions. The only thing we’ve changed is the application itself. Run: uv run python examples/experiment_comparison/compare_experiments.py \ --dataset-name wayfinder_experiment_comparison \ --prefix wayfinder-deterministic-filtering \ --repetitions 5 The runner creates a second experiment in LangSmith, this time using our candidate implementation. Now let’s look at the same multi-constraint request that failed once in our baseline: Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least 2 available seats. This time, all five repetitions receive a score of 5 across every evaluation criterion . In our baseline, the same request succeeded in four repetitions but selected the wrong flight in one. AI Engineering Fundamentals
AI Evaluation · Part 7

← Part 6

So far in this series, we have focused on one fundamental question:

How good is our AI application?

We started with deterministic checks, brought humans into the evaluation loop, used LLMs as judges, and eventually evaluated interactions happening in production.

But evaluation becomes even more useful when we start changing the application.

Maybe we changed the prompt. Maybe we switched models. Maybe we added a tool, changed retrieval, or moved part of the decision-making from the LLM into application code.

Now the question is different:

Did the change actually make the application better?

Running a few prompts against the new version and checking whether the responses look good isn’t enough. A change might improve the behavior we were targeting while quietly breaking something that already worked. And with non-deterministic AI systems, even running the same example once can give us a misleading picture.

The dataset stays the same. The evaluation criteria stay the same. The evaluator stays the same.

The application change is the variable we want to measure.

In this final part of the AI Evaluation series, we’ll do exactly that with Wayfinder our flight search application. We’ll establish a baseline, make a targeted engineering change, run the same evaluations again, and compare the experiments to understand not just whether the scores changed, but what behavior changed and whether the evidence is strong enough to support our engineering decision.

Building a Focused Dataset for the Comparison

But an overall score doesn’t always tell us what happened to the behavior we actually changed.

Imagine we make a change to improve how an AI application handles requests with multiple constraints. The overall evaluation score improves.

That sounds promising. But it leaves us with more important questions:

Did the behavior we wanted to improve actually get better? And did that change break anything that was already working?

To answer those questions, it helps to include examples that directly exercise the behavior we’re changing, along with examples that protect behavior that already works.

This gives us two useful types of evaluation cases:

Target case — exercises the behavior we expect our change to improve.

Regression guard — exercises behavior that already works and that we don’t want our change to break.

These focused cases don’t replace the application’s broader evaluation suite. They give us a clearer way to understand the impact of a particular change.

Throughout this series, we’ve used Wayfinder our AI-powered flight search assistant, to build and explore different evaluation techniques. We’ll continue with the same application here as we move into experiment comparison.

Consider this request:

Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least available seats.

Wayfinder has to do two things correctly here.

First, it needs to consider only flights with at least two available seats. Then, from those flights, it needs to find the cheapest one.

This is the behavior we want to study, so we’ll make it our target case.

But there is another side to the comparison.

Suppose our change fixes this request but somehow breaks a simpler request that Wayfinder already handles correctly:

What is the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow?

We haven’t really made the application better — we’ve just moved the problem somewhere else.

So we’ll keep this simpler request as a regression guard.

Our comparison dataset is therefore deliberately small:

{"id": "cheapest_with_min_seats",
 "query": "Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least 2 available seats.",
 "expected_behavior": "Recommend the lowest-priced retrieved flight that satisfies the stated minimum seat requirement. Do not recommend a more expensive flight when a cheaper eligible flight exists."}

{"id": "find_cheapest_flight",
 "query": "What is the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow?",
 "expected_behavior": "Recommend the lowest-priced retrieved flight for the requested route and date."}

The first case asks:

Did we improve the behavior we were trying to change?

The second asks:

Did we accidentally break behavior that already worked?

Of course, two examples are not enough to evaluate an entire AI application. That’s not what we’re trying to do here. We already built broader evaluation coverage earlier in the series.

For this experiment, these two cases give us a focused way to follow one change and understand its impact.

And most importantly, we won’t change them between experiments.

We’ll first run them against the current version of the application to establish a baseline. Later, after making our change, we’ll run the exact same examples again and compare the results.

With the dataset fixed, we now need a way to run those evaluations as repeatable experiments.

Running the Experiment Locally
If you’ve been following the series and already have Wayfinder set up locally, you can skip the installation and environment setup below. Just make sure you’re on the version used for this experiment.

The complete implementation used throughout this article is available in the companion GitHub repository. To follow along with exactly the same code shown in this article, check out the v0.6.0 release. This ensures the code, commands and screenshots remain consistent over time.

To follow along locally, clone the repository and check out the release containing the online evaluation implementation:

git clone https://github.com/DivakarUngatla/wayfinder.git
cd wayfinder
git checkout v0.6.0

Install the project dependencies:

uv sync

Before running the evaluation, configure the required environment variables.

Create a .env file:

cp .env.example .env

Configure the required environment variables:

OPENAI_API_KEY=
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
Running Evaluations as Experiments

We now have a fixed set of examples. The next step is to run them against the application and record the results in a way that lets us compare them later.

We’ll do that by running the evaluation as an experiment.

An experiment is a recorded evaluation run of a particular version of our application against a fixed dataset.

For each example, the experiment:

  1. runs the application
  2. captures its response and the context it used
  3. evaluates that response
  4. records the results

Later, after we change the application, we’ll repeat the same experiment with the same evaluation setup and compare the results.

For Wayfinder, we’ve wrapped this workflow in a small experiment runner:

def target(inputs):
    result = agent.run(inputs["query"])

    return {
        "response": result.response,
        "retrieved_flights": [
            flight.model_dump() for flight in result.flights
        ],
    }


def evaluator(run, example):
    return judge.evaluate(
        query=example.inputs["query"],
        expected_behavior=example.outputs["expected_behavior"],
        response=run.outputs["response"],
        context=run.outputs["retrieved_flights"],
    )

The target is the application we're evaluating. LangSmith gives it an example from our dataset, and Wayfinder returns both the generated response and the flights it retrieved.

The evaluator then takes that output and scores it against the expected behavior.

We’re reusing the same LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator we built earlier in the series, so we’re not introducing a new evaluation technique here. We’re changing how we use the evaluation results: instead of looking at one run in isolation, we’re going to compare runs from different versions of the application.

LangSmith’s evaluate() ties the pieces together:

evaluate(
    target,
    data=dataset_name,
    evaluators=[langsmith_llm_judge_evaluator],
    experiment_prefix=args.prefix,
    num_repetitions=args.repetitions,
)

The dataset gives us the examples. The target runs Wayfinder. The evaluator scores its behavior. And LangSmith records the results as an experiment that we can inspect and compare later.

There is one parameter here that deserves some attention:

num_repetitions=args.repetitions

Why would we run the same evaluation example more than once?

Because with an AI application, one successful run doesn’t necessarily mean the behavior is consistently correct.

And that’s something our baseline experiment is about to show us.

Establishing Our Baseline

Before making any changes to the application, we need to understand how the current version behaves. This gives us our baseline — the reference point we’ll compare our change against later.

We’ll run the two examples in our dataset five times each:

python examples/experiment_comparison/compare_experiments.py \
  --dataset-name wayfinder_experiment_comparison \
  --prefix wayfinder-baseline \
  --repetitions 5

The first time we run this command, the experiment runner creates the dataset in LangSmith from our local JSONL file. From then on, we’ll reuse this same dataset for every experiment in this article.

With two examples and five repetitions, our baseline contains 10 evaluation runs.

Why repeat each example five times instead of evaluating it once?

Because a single successful response can give us a false sense of confidence. AI applications can produce different responses for the same input, and our LLM-based evaluator can vary as well.

If a behavior works once, we know it can work.

If it works repeatedly, we start learning something about how consistently it works.

When the evaluation completes, the runner prints a link to the experiment in LangSmith. Let’s open it and look at what happened across the five repetitions.

The simple cheapest-flight request works correctly in all five runs. The multi-constraint request is different: four repetitions score perfectly, but one fails.

In repetition 3, Wayfinder recommends Japan Airlines JL703 at ₹48,550 with 12 available seats.

But the retrieved flights also contain Air India AI302 at ₹41,000 with 6 available seats. Air India satisfies the same minimum-seat requirement and is cheaper.

Wayfinder had the information it needed, but still selected the wrong flight.

Your exact results may differ. Both the application and the LLM-based evaluator are non-deterministic, so you may see the incorrect recommendation in a different repetition — or all five runs may succeed. What matters is that we use the same evaluation setup when comparing the baseline with the version we change next.

The interesting part isn’t that Wayfinder cannot handle the request — it gets it right in four of the five runs.

The problem is that the same request doesn’t produce consistently correct behavior.

Now we have something concrete to improve — and something concrete to compare our next experiment against.

Finding the Right Thing to Change

Our baseline showed us where the application sometimes fails. But before changing anything, we need to understand why.

In the failed run, Wayfinder had already retrieved the cheaper Air India flight. So retrieval wasn’t the problem.

The problem happens after retrieval.

In the current implementation, the retrieved flights are passed to the response-generation LLM. The LLM has to apply the user’s constraints, compare the eligible flights, select the cheapest one and generate the final response.

Conceptually, the flow looks like this:

Retrieved Flights
       ↓
      LLM
       ↓
Apply constraints
Compare prices
Generate response

But filtering by available seats and comparing prices are deterministic operations. We don’t need an LLM to make those decisions.

That gives us a simple engineering hypothesis:

Move deterministic filtering and ranking into application code, and let the LLM focus on generating the response.

The application would then look more like:

Retrieved Flights
       ↓
Filter + Rank
       ↓
      LLM
       ↓
Generate response

We don’t know yet whether this change will actually improve the application.

That’s exactly what our next experiment will measure.

Moving Deterministic Decisions into Application Code

Now we can implement our hypothesis.

Wayfinder already uses an LLM to convert the user’s request into a structured FlightSearchRequest. We can extend that structure so the application also knows how the results should be ranked:

passengers: int = Field(default=1)

sort_by: Literal["price", "duration"] | None = None
arrival_before: time | None = None

For our target request:

Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least 2 available seats.

the extraction step now produces:

{
  "source": "Bangalore",
  "destination": "Tokyo",
  "passengers": 2,
  "sort_by": "price",
  "arrival_before": null
}

The LLM is still doing something it’s good at: turning natural language into structured intent.

But once we have that structure, the application can handle the deterministic decisions itself:

flights = [
    flight for flight in flights
    if flight.available_seats >= request.passengers
]

if request.sort_by == "price":
    flights.sort(key=lambda flight: flight.price)
elif request.sort_by == "duration":
    flights.sort(key=lambda flight: flight.duration)

For our target request, this means Wayfinder first removes flights with fewer than two available seats and then sorts the remaining flights by price.

The response-generation LLM no longer needs to perform that filtering or ranking itself. It receives flights that have already been processed according to the structured request and focuses on generating the response.

So our architecture has shifted from:

LLM → interpret constraints + make deterministic decisions + respond

to:

LLM → structured intent → deterministic application logic → LLM response

The change looks promising, but we haven’t established that it actually improves the application’s behavior.

To find out, we’ll run the same evaluation again and compare the two experiments

We’ve only looked at the key parts of the change here. The complete implementation also handles additional filtering and ranking behavior and updates the response-generation flow accordingly.

If you’re following along with the repository, switch back to the main branch to get the completed candidate implementation:

git checkout main
git pull

This gives us the candidate version we’ll evaluate next. Our v0.6.0 checkout remains the reproducible baseline we started with.

Running the Candidate Experiment

Now we evaluate the changed application using exactly the same setup as our baseline.

Same dataset. Same two examples. Same evaluator. Same five repetitions.

The only thing we’ve changed is the application itself.

Run:

uv run python examples/experiment_comparison/compare_experiments.py \
  --dataset-name wayfinder_experiment_comparison \
  --prefix wayfinder-deterministic-filtering \
  --repetitions 5

The runner creates a second experiment in LangSmith, this time using our candidate implementation.

Now let’s look at the same multi-constraint request that failed once in our baseline:

Find the cheapest flight from Bangalore to Tokyo tomorrow with at least 2 available seats.

This time, all five repetitions receive a score of 5 across every evaluation criterion.

In our baseline, the same request succeeded in four repetitions but selected the wrong flight in one. After moving filtering and ranking into deterministic application logic, we don’t see that failure in any of the five candidate repetitions.

That’s encouraging — but looking at the candidate experiment by itself still doesn’t answer the question we started this article with.

Did our change actually make the application better overall?

For that, we need to compare the baseline and candidate experiments directly.

Comparing the Experiments

Now we can finally put the two experiments side by side.

Both experiments used the same dataset, evaluator, and five repetitions per example. The only thing we intentionally changed was the application.

LangSmith lets us compare the results directly:

For our multi-constraint request, the difference is immediately visible.

The baseline’s failed repetition pulled several evaluation scores down. In the candidate experiment, every criterion scores 5.00 across all five repetitions.

More importantly, the behavior changed: we no longer observed the incorrect flight selection, while our simpler cheapest-flight regression guard continued to work correctly.

The behavior we targeted improved, while the behavior we wanted to protect did not regress.

This doesn’t prove the application will behave correctly for every request. But with the same dataset, evaluator, and repetitions on both sides, we now have evidence that our change improved the behavior we set out to fix.

That’s what experiment comparison gives us: evidence for an engineering decision.

Conclusion

In this article, we explored how evaluation experiments can help us answer a question that comes up constantly when building AI applications:

Did my change actually make the application better?

We built a focused evaluation dataset, established a baseline across repeated runs, made a targeted application change, and evaluated the candidate using the same setup.

By comparing the two experiments, we could see whether the behavior we wanted to improve actually got better while also checking that existing behavior didn’t regress.

This gives us a repeatable engineering loop for changing AI applications:

Baseline → Change → Evaluate → Compare → Decide

Whether we’re changing prompts, models, retrieval, tools, or application logic, experiment comparison gives us evidence to understand the impact of those changes instead of relying on intuition or a few successful examplesison gives us a way to answer that question with evidence.

What’s Next?

With experiment comparison, we’ve completed the AI Evaluation track of AI Engineering Fundamentals.

Across this series, we’ve moved from understanding why traditional software tests aren’t enough for AI applications to building rule-based, human, LLM-based, and online evaluation workflows — and finally to using those evaluations to measure the impact of application changes.

Next, we’ll move on to the next area of AI engineering.

items.summary:
When we examine the modern enterprise AI landscape, we frequently encounter a common paradox: while generative AI promises to revolutionize customer support, internal search, and knowledge management, the underlying infrastructure required to deploy these solutions often grows prohibitively complex. Historically, building a production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline meant provisioning specialized external vector databases, managing intricate data synchronization pipelines, and risking data sprawl across ungoverned cloud environments. We realized that for many enterprise workloads, this massive infrastructure overhead is entirely unnecessary. By leveraging Microsoft Fabric ’s unified data estate, native Apache Spark engine, and Delta Lake storage format, we can build a fully operational, enterprise-grade RAG solution directly on top of our existing OneLake data. In this detailed operational guide, we share how we designed and deployed an end-to-end vector embedding and retrieval system using fewer than 50 lines of PySpark and Python code, connecting Azure OpenAI directly to our governed customer transcripts without moving a single byte outside our analytical perimeter. Architecture: OneLake → PySpark Vectorization → Azure OpenAI Our primary goal was to design an architecture that maximizes simplicity, security, and query execution performance while operating entirely within our governed workspace. Rather than exporting unstructured transcripts to a third-party vector database, we construct a unified pipeline where storage, compute, and AI inference coexist seamlessly. Our end-to-end RAG workflow follows a structured four-stage continuum: Governed Storage Layer (OneLake & Delta Parquet): Our raw and processed datasets, such as customer support logs, operational records, or internal knowledge bases reside directly within our Lakehouse as open Delta Parquet tables. This guarantees ACID compliance, version history, and zero-copy accessibility across analytical engines. Distributed Vectorization Engine (PySpark & Pandas UDFs): We harness Fabric’s native Apache Spark compute cluster to distribute the task of generating vector embeddings across millions of text records simultaneously. By employing PyArrow-accelerated Pandas UDFs, we batch API requests to Azure OpenAI efficiently. In-Lake Vector Persistence: Vector embeddings are stored natively as array columns inside a dedicated Gold Delta table (Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors). This eliminates external database licensing costs and guarantees that vector updates maintain strict transactional synchronization with our source tables. Distributed Vector Retrieval & Downstream Serving: We query our vectorized Delta tables directly using high-performance Spark mathematical expressions to extract relevant context segments, which are then passed alongside user prompts to Azure OpenAI or surfaced through interactive interfaces. Generating Embeddings: Distributed Processing with Pandas UDFs To transform raw, unstructured text into dense vector representations, we must process large volumes of data efficiently. Calling an external embedding API row-by-row in a traditional loop introduces severe latency bottlenecks and exhausts network bandwidth. To resolve this, we leverage PySpark’s vectorized Pandas User Defined Functions (@pandas_udf). Pandas UDFs utilize Apache Arrow to transfer data seamlessly between Spark JVM memory and Python worker processes without the performance penalty of standard Python serialization. This allows us to process incoming text series in batched chunks, optimizing worker throughput and stabilizing API call patterns. Below is the exact implementation we designed to read customer support transcripts from OneLake, generate 1536-dimensional vector embeddings using Azure OpenAI, and persist the results back into our Gold Lakehouse layer: # PySpark Notebook in Fabric: Creating Vector Embeddings for OneLake Text Data import openai from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf, col import pandas as pd # Set Azure OpenAI Config openai.api_type = "azure" openai.api_base = "https://your-resource.openai.azure.com/" openai.api_key = "YOUR_KEY" # Define a Pandas UDF for batch embedding generation @pandas_udf("array ") def generate_embeddings(text_series: pd.Series) -> pd.Series: def get_embedding(text): response = openai.Embedding.create( input=text, engine="text-embedding-ada-002" ) return response['data'][0]['embedding'] return text_series.apply(get_embedding) ' # Read customer support logs from OneLake df_logs = spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.CustomerSupportTranscripts") # Generate embeddings and save as a new Delta table for vector search df_vectorized = df_logs.withColumn("VectorEmbedding", generate_embeddings(col("TranscriptText"))) df_vectorized.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors") Deconstructing the Vectorization Pipeline Let us examine the mechanical steps executed by this concise script: Environment Configuration: We initialize our Azure OpenAI credentials and endpoint configurations directly within our secure Fabric Notebook execution session. Vectorized UDF Definition: By decorating our function with @pandas_udf("array "), we instruct PySpark that the output column will be structured as an array of floating-point values. The inner function accepts a pandas.Series containing text fragments and dispatches API requests to the text-embedding-ada-002 model. Reading Governed Delta Tables: We invoke spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.CustomerSupportTranscripts") to fetch our curated support transcripts natively from OneLake. Fabric abstracts away underlying ABFSS file paths and partition handling automatically. Distributed Transformation: When we execute withColumn("VectorEmbedding", generate_embeddings(...)), PySpark distributes the workload across the active Spark cluster nodes. Each executor node processes a slice of the dataset in parallel, sending batched requests to Azure OpenAI. Atomic Delta Lake Persistence: Finally, we persist the vectorized DataFrame back into OneLake using .write.format("delta").saveAsTable("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors"). Because Delta Lake provides strict ACID transaction guarantees, our vectorized dataset remains resilient against partial failures during write operations. Vector Search: Querying Embeddings Using PySpark & Math Functions Once our text embeddings are persisted in OneLake, we require a method to identify the most relevant customer transcripts when an incoming user query arrives. In traditional RAG setups, this step relies on dedicated vector databases using index structures like HNSW or IVF. However, for datasets containing hundreds of thousands to millions of rows, we can compute mathematical similarity directly within PySpark using vector geometry. Cosine similarity is the gold standard metric for measuring semantic closeness between high-dimensional text embeddings. Conceptually, it evaluates the angle between two vectors, such as an incoming user query and a stored document to determine how similar they are in context. Distributed Vector Lookup in PySpark We can implement this similarity lookup natively by taking an incoming user prompt, generating its vector representation, and computing the dot product against our vector column stored in Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors: # PySpark Vector Retrieval Code import numpy as np from pyspark.sql.functions import udf, col from pyspark.sql.types import FloatType # 1. Generate query embedding for user prompt user_prompt = "How do I reset my customer portal password?" prompt_response = openai.Embedding.create(input=user_prompt, engine="text-embedding-ada-002") query_vector = prompt_response['data'][0]['embedding'] # 2. Define a cosine similarity / dot product UDF @udf(returnType=FloatType()) def compute_similarity(doc_vector): if doc_vector is None: return 0.0 return float(np.dot(query_vector, doc_vector)) # 3. Query vectors from OneLake and retrieve top 5 matches df_vectors = spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors") top_matches = ( df_vectors .withColumn("Similarity", compute_similarity(col("VectorEmbedding"))) .orderBy(col("Similarity").desc()) .limit(5) ) # Collect top context documents retrieved_docs = [row['TranscriptText'] for row in top_matches.collect()] By executing this transformation across our Spark cluster, we perform candidate vector retrieval directly inside our analytical Lakehouse engine. The process retrieves the most contextually relevant transcript segments within milliseconds, perfectly preparing our pipeline for the generative synthesis stage. Serving and Orchestration: Synthesizing Context and Deployment With our vector retrieval engine operational, the final component of our enterprise RAG pipeline is prompt orchestration and response generation. We synthesize the retrieved transcript passages into a grounded context window and submit the instruction to Azure OpenAI Chat Completions. # Construct grounded context prompt context_block = "
---
".join(retrieved_docs) system_instruction = ( "We are an AI assistant designed to answer customer support queries based strictly on historic logs. " "Use only the provided context to answer the prompt accurately." ) # Call Azure OpenAI Chat Completion completion_response = openai.ChatCompletion.create( engine="gpt-4", messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": system_instruction}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:
{context_block}

Question: {user_prompt}"} ] ) final_answer = completion_response['choices'][0]['message']['content'] print(final_answer) Deployment Patterns: Gradio and Copilot Studio Integrations To bring this RAG solution into production and surface it to business stakeholders across our organization, we evaluate two highly effective serving patterns: Embedded Interactive Interfaces in Fabric: For internal prototyping, testing, or technical user interfaces, we can wrap our retrieval and synthesis functions into a lightweight Gradio interface running directly within a Fabric Notebook session. This allows analysts to test context retrieval, adjust hyper-parameters, and evaluate model grounding in real time. Copilot Studio & Semantic Link Orchestration: For enterprise-wide deployment, we can expose our PySpark RAG execution logic as an automated backend endpoint or register our Lakehouse tables within Power BI semantic models using Semantic Link (sempy). Copilot Studio can then query these semantic layers and invoke our underlying vectorized tables seamlessly, providing business users with an AI agent that converses with governed enterprise data in real time. Production Considerations: Performance, Cost, and Governance As we transition our concise PySpark RAG pipeline into a continuous production environment, we incorporate several critical engineering practices to maintain operational efficiency and low compute cost: Storage Optimization with V-Order: When saving our vectorized Delta tables in OneLake, we ensure that Microsoft’s proprietary V-Order compression is enabled. V-Order reorganizes Parquet files at write time, dramatically improving memory layout and accelerating downstream read speeds when Spark or SQL engines scan vector arrays. Incremental Embeddings via Change Data Capture (CDC): Rather than re-generating embeddings for our entire dataset during every run, we implement incremental processing using Delta Lake transaction logs. By inspecting modified rows, we only vectorize newly inserted or updated customer transcripts, reducing OpenAI API overhead substantially. Unified Data Governance & Security: Because our embeddings reside within native OneLake Delta tables, they inherit Microsoft Purview governance policies, row-level security, and access controls automatically. Sensitive customer information remains fully safeguarded without requiring complex vector database role-based access configurations. Conclusion By unifying our storage layer, distributed compute, vector geometry, and generative AI orchestration within Microsoft Fabric , we eliminate the friction of managing external infrastructure. In under 50 lines of Python code, we constructed a resilient, enterprise-grade RAG pipeline that operates entirely on top of open Delta Parquet tables in OneLake. This architecture keeps our enterprise data fully governed, minimizes total cost of ownership, and accelerates our time-to-value when deploying generative AI solutions. Rather than exporting unstructured transcripts to a third-party vector database, we construct a unified pipeline where storage, compute, and AI inference coexist seamlessly.

  • Distributed Vectorization Engine (PySpark & Pandas UDFs): We harness Fabric’s native Apache Spark compute cluster to distribute the task of generating vector embeddings across millions of text records simultaneously. By employing PyArrow-accelerated Pandas UDFs, we batch API requests to Azure OpenAI efficiently.
  • In-Lake Vector Persistence: Vector embeddings are stored natively as array columns inside a dedicated Gold Delta table (Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors). This eliminates external database licensing costs and guarantees that vector updates maintain strict transactional synchronization with our source tables.
  • Distributed Vector Retrieval & Downstream Serving: We query our vectorized Delta tables directly using high-performance Spark mathematical expressions to extract relevant context segments, which are then passed alongside user prompts to Azure OpenAI or surfaced through interactive interfaces.
Generating Embeddings: Distributed Processing with Pandas UDFs

To transform raw, unstructured text into dense vector representations, we must process large volumes of data efficiently. Calling an external embedding API row-by-row in a traditional loop introduces severe latency bottlenecks and exhausts network bandwidth. To resolve this, we leverage PySpark’s vectorized Pandas User Defined Functions (@pandas_udf).

Pandas UDFs utilize Apache Arrow to transfer data seamlessly between Spark JVM memory and Python worker processes without the performance penalty of standard Python serialization. This allows us to process incoming text series in batched chunks, optimizing worker throughput and stabilizing API call patterns.

import pandas as pd

# Set Azure OpenAI Config

openai.api_base = "https://your-resource.openai.azure.com/"
openai.api_key = "YOUR_KEY"

# Define a Pandas UDF for batch embedding generation
@pandas_udf("array")
def generate_embeddings(text_series: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    def get_embedding(text):
        response = openai.Embedding.create(
            input=text, engine="text-embedding-ada-002"
        )
        return response['data'][0]['embedding']
    return text_series.apply(get_embedding)
'
# Read customer support logs from OneLake
df_logs = spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.CustomerSupportTranscripts")

# Generate embeddings and save as a new Delta table for vector search
df_vectorized = df_logs.withColumn("VectorEmbedding", generate_embeddings(col("TranscriptText")))
df_vectorized.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors")
Deconstructing the Vectorization Pipeline

Let us examine the mechanical steps executed by this concise script:

  • Environment Configuration: We initialize our Azure OpenAI credentials and endpoint configurations directly within our secure Fabric Notebook execution session.
  • Vectorized UDF Definition: By decorating our function with @pandas_udf("array"), we instruct PySpark that the output column will be structured as an array of floating-point values.   • Reading Governed Delta Tables: We invoke spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.CustomerSupportTranscripts") to fetch our curated support transcripts natively from OneLake. Fabric abstracts away underlying ABFSS file paths and partition handling automatically.
  • Distributed Transformation: When we execute withColumn("VectorEmbedding", generate_embeddings(...)), PySpark distributes the workload across the active Spark cluster nodes. Each executor node processes a slice of the dataset in parallel, sending batched requests to Azure OpenAI.
  • Atomic Delta Lake Persistence: Finally, we persist the vectorized DataFrame back into OneLake using .write.format("delta").saveAsTable("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors"). Because Delta Lake provides strict ACID transaction guarantees, our vectorized dataset remains resilient against partial failures during write operations.
Vector Search: Querying Embeddings Using PySpark & Math Functions

Once our text embeddings are persisted in OneLake, we require a method to identify the most relevant customer transcripts when an incoming user query arrives. In traditional RAG setups, this step relies on dedicated vector databases using index structures like HNSW or IVF. However, for datasets containing hundreds of thousands to millions of rows, we can compute mathematical similarity directly within PySpark using vector geometry.

Cosine similarity is the gold standard metric for measuring semantic closeness between high-dimensional text embeddings. Conceptually, it evaluates the angle between two vectors, such as an incoming user query and a stored document to determine how similar they are in context.

Distributed Vector Lookup in PySpark

We can implement this similarity lookup natively by taking an incoming user prompt, generating its vector representation, and computing the dot product against our vector column stored in Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors:

# PySpark Vector Retrieval Code
import numpy as np
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf, col
from pyspark.sql.types import FloatType

# 1. Generate query embedding for user prompt
user_prompt = "How do I reset my customer portal password?"
prompt_response = openai.Embedding.create(input=user_prompt, engine="text-embedding-ada-002")
query_vector = prompt_response['data'][0]['embedding']

# 2. Define a cosine similarity / dot product UDF
@udf(returnType=FloatType())
def compute_similarity(doc_vector):
    if doc_vector is None:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.dot(query_vector, doc_vector))

# 3. Query vectors from OneLake and retrieve top 5 matches
df_vectors = spark.read.table("Gold_Lakehouse.SupportVectors")
top_matches = (
    df_vectors
    .withColumn("Similarity", compute_similarity(col("VectorEmbedding")))
    .orderBy(col("Similarity").desc())
    .limit(5)
)

# Collect top context documents
retrieved_docs = [row['TranscriptText'] for row in top_matches.collect()]

By executing this transformation across our Spark cluster, we perform candidate vector retrieval directly inside our analytical Lakehouse engine. With our vector retrieval engine operational, the final component of our enterprise RAG pipeline is prompt orchestration and response generation. We synthesize the retrieved transcript passages into a grounded context window and submit the instruction to Azure OpenAI Chat Completions.

{context_block}
